body_ar:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين يقول المؤلف رحمه الله تعالى: باب معرفة الوقوف عقد هذا الباب لبيان أمر مهم من أمور التجويد وهو حكم الوقف والابتداء، والوقف في اللغة مصدر وقف تستعمل لازمة وتستعمل متعدية، فيقال وقف فلان في الصلاة أي قام، ويقال وقف فلان راحلته أو ناقته إذا حبسها، ومنه قول عنترة

ولقد وقفت بها طويلا ناقتي** أشكو إلى سفع رواكد جثم

وقول امرئ القيس:

وقوفا بها صحبي علي مطيهم** يقولون لا تهلك أسى وتجمل

ونظيره قول طرفة:

وقوفا بها صحبي علي مطيهم** يقولون لا تهلك أسى وتجلد
body_en:
In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. I pray for blessing and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and all who are guided by his guidance and follow his sunnah until the Day of Judgement.

The author says, may God Most High have mercy on him: "Chapter on the knowledge of the stopping-places." He set out this chapter to explain an important matter among the matters of recitation, namely the ruling on stopping (waqf) and on beginning (ibtidāʾ). Waqf in the language is the verbal noun of waqafa, which is used intransitively and is used transitively. One says "so-and-so waqafa in the prayer", meaning he stood; and one says "so-and-so waqafa his mount or his she-camel", meaning he brought it to a halt. From this is the saying of ʿAntarah:

*And long did I halt my she-camel there, making my complaint to blackened hearth-stones, motionless and crouching.*

And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*My companions halted their mounts over me there, saying: do not perish of grief; bear yourself well.*

And its counterpart, the saying of Tarafah:

*My companions halted their mounts over me there, saying: do not perish of grief; be steadfast.*

flags.context: the line attributed to ʿAntarah, cited to illustrate the transitive use of waqafa
options: translate as printed, with waqaftu ('I halted')
translate as printed and note that the received line reads ḥabastu
flags.note: PROBABLE MISQUOTATION IN THE SOURCE, and a consequential one. The line as it is received in ʿAntarah's muʿallaqah reads wa-la-qad ḥabastu bihā ṭawīlan nāqatī — 'and long did I hold back my she-camel there'. The source has waqaftu in place of ḥabastu. That substitution matters because the line is being cited for the express purpose of proving that waqafa takes a direct object; if the verb in the line is in fact ḥabasa, the line does not prove the point. This may be the Sheikh quoting from memory, as the style guide warns is common in this tradition, or a transcription slip, or a deliberate paraphrase to make the point. It is translated as printed and must not be repaired; a reviewer with the audio should establish which it is, and the answer affects whether the argument stands as published.

flags.arabic: وقوفا بها صحبي علي مطيهم ** يقولون لا تهلك أسى وتجمل / ... وتجلد
flags.context: two lines given as counterparts, from Imru' al-Qays and from Tarafah
options: render the two closing words distinctly, as 'bear yourself well' and 'be steadfast'
keep tajammal and tajallad in transliteration
flags.note: The two lines are identical but for the final word, which is the reason the Sheikh pairs them, so the English must keep the two words distinct or the pairing becomes pointless repetition. Tajammul is composure and bearing oneself becomingly; tajallud is endurance and fortitude. The lines are correctly attributed in the source: both muʿallaqāt do carry them.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The date shown by the CMS is a bulk-upload timestamp shared by every item in this range, not the date the Sheikh gave the answer. The real date of composition is unknown. See date_is_cms_bulk_upload.

This record belongs to the Sheikh's commentary on the Muqaddimah al-Jazariyyah, Ibn al-Jazari's versified primer on the rules of Qur'anic recitation. The CMS holds the tapes out of order across ids 641–646 and the part numbers in the titles do not run with the ids; the series should be ordered by the number in the title, not by id.

EXCERPT ONLY. The published text breaks off and the full material is offered as a .docx download ('taḥmīl al-māddah'). The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. The download-link label has been removed from body_ar as a navigation element and recorded in source_download_link.
The record breaks off immediately after the third line of verse, with no download-label sentence of its own beyond the standard one.

Per the style guide the three lines of verse are rendered as prose in italics, with the Arabic kept in the bilingual pane; no rhymed English has been attempted. The doubled asterisks in the source are hemistich separators.

'Blackened hearth-stones, motionless and crouching' renders sufʿ rawākid juthṭham — the fire-blackened stones of an abandoned camp, a standing image of the deserted encampment in this poetry. The image has been kept rather than explained away.

The grammatical point being made is that waqafa is both intransitive ('to stand') and transitive ('to halt something'), which is why the Arabic verb has been kept in the two illustrative sentences instead of being replaced by two different English verbs.
